p.src: Now Sun the Great Sage struggled about for a while inside the old demon's belly. The monster fell to the ground, silent and breathless. Thinking him dead when he did not speak, the Great Sage eased his hand. The monster recovered his breath and cried, “O merciful and compassionate Bodhisattva, Great Sage Equal to Heaven!” Hearing this, the Pilgrim said, “Son, do not waste your breath. Save yourself a few words and simply call me Grandpa Sun.” The demon valued his life and truly called out, “Grandpa! Grandpa! I was in the wrong. By an unfortunate mistake I swallowed you, and now you are harming me in return. I earnestly beg the Great Sage to show mercy, pity even an ant's longing for life, and spare me. I promise to escort your master across the mountain.” Hero though the Great Sage was, he cared deeply about advancing Tang Monk on his journey. Seeing the demon plead so piteously, and being one who liked a little flattery, he softened and called, “Monster, I will spare you—but how will you escort my master?” The old demon said, “We have no rare treasures here to offer you—no gold or silver, pearls or jadeite, agate, coral, crystal, amber, or tortoiseshell. Instead, we three brothers will carry your master across this mountain in a fragrant rattan sedan chair.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Being escorted in a sedan chair is better than receiving treasure. Open your mouth and let me out.” The monster duly opened his mouth. The third demon came near and whispered to the old demon, “Elder Brother, when he comes out, snap your jaws shut, chew the monkey to pieces, and swallow him. Then he will no longer torment you.”

p.src: The Pilgrim had heard this from within. Instead of coming out first, he thrust out his gold-banded cudgel to test the monster. Sure enough, the monster bit down. There was a sharp crack, and all his front teeth shattered. The Pilgrim drew back his cudgel and said, “Fine monster! I spared your life and meant to come out, yet you tried to bite me and take my life. I will not come out. I shall torment you to death from within. I will not come out! I will not!” The old demon complained to the third, “Brother, you have made one of our own turn against another. It would have been best simply to invite him out, but you told me to bite him. Not only did I fail to bite him, but the blow has left my gums aching. What are we to do now?”

p.src: When the third demon saw the old demon blame him, he tried a taunt instead and shouted fiercely, “Sun the Pilgrim! I had heard your name like thunder ringing in my ears. They say you displayed your might outside the Southern Gate of Heaven, flaunted your power below the Hall of Miraculous Mist, and now subdue demons and bind monsters on the road to the Western Heaven. Yet you are only a cowardly little monkey after all.” The Pilgrim said, “What makes me a cowardly youngster?” The third monster replied, “‘A fine traveler is admired for a thousand miles; his fame is carried ten thousand.’ Come out and fight me. Only then will you be a true hero. What sort of deed is it to skulk inside another's belly? If that does not make you a cowardly youngster, what does?” Hearing this, the Pilgrim thought to himself, “True, true, true. What difficulty would there be in tearing out his intestines, crushing his liver, and tormenting this monster to death right now? But it truly would stain my reputation. Very well, very well! Open your mouth, and I will come out to match myself against you. But the entrance to your cave is cramped, with no room to wield my weapon. We must go somewhere open.” Hearing this, the third demon mustered monsters great and small. More than thirty thousand fiends, all bearing keen weapons, marched out of the cave and deployed in the formation of Heaven, Earth, and Man, waiting solely for the Pilgrim to emerge so they could attack together. The second monster supported the old demon and led him straight outside. They called, “Sun the Pilgrim, come out if you are a hero! Here is an open battlefield fit for combat.”

p.src: From inside his belly, the Great Sage heard crows cawing, magpies chattering, cranes crying, and the wind sighing, and knew they had reached an open place. Then he thought, “If I do not go out, I shall have broken my word to him; but if I do, this fiend has a human face and a beast's heart. First he promised to escort my master, then tricked me into coming out so he could bite me, and now he has assembled troops here. Very well, very well. I shall find a way to satisfy both sides: I will go out, but leave a root growing inside his belly.” He reached back, plucked a hair from his tail, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly changed into a cord no thicker than a hair, yet some forty zhang long. He paid out the cord, and as soon as it met the wind, it grew thick. He tied one end around the demon's heart and liver with a running noose. The noose remained loose when not pulled, but tightened painfully whenever it was tugged. Holding the other end, he laughed and said, “Once I am out, all will be well if he escorts my master; but if he refuses and resorts to arms, I need waste no time fighting him. A single pull on this cord will be just as effective as if I were still inside his belly.” He then made his body tiny and began crawling out. When he reached below the throat, he saw the demon's square mouth gaping wide, its upper and lower rows of steel teeth arrayed like sharp blades. Suddenly he thought, “This is bad, very bad! If I go out through his mouth while pulling this cord, the pain may make him bite down and sever it. I will leave through a place where he has no teeth.” Splendid Great Sage! Paying out the cord, he crawled forward along the monster's upper palate until he reached a nostril. The old demon's nose began to itch. With a loud “Achoo!” he sneezed and blasted the Pilgrim straight out.

p.src: Once the Pilgrim felt the wind, he bent his waist and grew to a height of some three zhang, holding the cord in one hand and his iron cudgel in the other. The monster, unable to tell good from ill, raised his steel saber the moment he saw the Pilgrim emerge and hacked straight at his face. The Great Sage met the blow with the iron cudgel in one hand. Then the second monster attacked with his spear and the third with his halberd, all striking wildly from every side. The Great Sage slackened the cord, put away his iron cudgel, and hurriedly sprang up on a cloud and departed. He feared that the swarm of lesser demons would surround him and hamper his work. He leaped beyond their encampment, flew to a broad, open hilltop, and descended from his cloud. Gripping the cord with both hands, he gave it a mighty pull, and only then did pain seize the old demon's heart. Writhing in pain, the demon struggled upward, and the Great Sage pulled downward once more. Seeing this from afar, all the lesser demons cried in unison, “Your Majesty, do not provoke him! Let him go. That monkey has no regard for the season. The Qingming Festival has not even arrived, yet there he is already flying a kite!” Hearing this, the Great Sage planted his feet and gave a powerful yank. With a great flapping and clattering, the old demon came tumbling from the sky like a spinning wheel and crashed into the dust. He struck the hard yellow earth below the slope with such force that he made a pit two feet deep.

p.src: The second and third fiends were so alarmed that they both lowered their clouds, rushed forward, seized the rope, and knelt below the slope, pleading, “Great Sage! We had thought you an immortal of boundless generosity, but who knew you were such a petty, narrow-minded fellow? We truly did deceive you into coming out to face us in battle, but we never expected you to fasten a rope around our elder brother’s heart.” Pilgrim laughed. “You insolent fiends are utterly unreasonable. Last time you lured me out and bit me; this time you lured me out again and arrayed your forces against me. For tens of thousands of demon soldiers to fight me alone is hardly fair. I’ll drag him away—drag him before my master.” The fiends all kowtowed and said, “Have mercy, Great Sage! Spare our lives, and we shall escort your venerable master across the mountain.” Pilgrim laughed. “If you want to live, simply take a knife and cut the rope.” The old fiend cried, “Grandfather! Even if we cut the part outside, the part within is tied around my heart, and something is making me retch in my throat. What am I to do?” Pilgrim said, “In that case, open your mouth and let me go back inside to untie it.” The old fiend panicked. “If you go in again and refuse to come out, that would be disastrous—truly disastrous!” Pilgrim said, “I have the skill to untie the inner end of the rope from out here. But once I untie it, will you truly escort my master?” The old fiend said, “Untie it and we shall escort him. We would never dare lie to you.” Having judged that he spoke sincerely, the Great Sage gave his body a shake and recalled the hairs. At once the fiend’s heart ceased to hurt. This had been a deceptive trick of the Great Sage Sun: he had used one of his hairs to bind the fiend’s heart, so when he recalled the hair, the pain naturally stopped. The three fiends sprang up and said in thanks, “Please return, Great Sage, and tell the Tang Monk to pack his luggage. We shall bring a sedan chair at once to escort him.” The host of fiends laid down their weapons and all returned to the cave.

p.src: The Great Sage gathered up the rope and went straight back to the eastern side of the mountain. From afar he saw the Tang Monk rolling on the ground and weeping bitterly, while Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk had opened the bundles and were dividing up the luggage between them. Pilgrim sighed inwardly. “There is no need to ask. Bajie must have told Master that the fiend ate me, and Master, unable to bear losing me, is weeping bitterly; and that idiot is dividing the possessions before the party breaks up. Well! I wonder if that is truly what happened. Let me call out and see.” He lowered his cloud and called, “Master!” Hearing him, Sha Monk reproached Bajie: “You accursed bearer of coffins—you do nothing but bring harm upon others! Elder Brother was never dead, yet you said he was and carried on with this business here. Haven’t you called him back by doing so?” Bajie said, “I saw clearly that the fiend swallowed him in one gulp. The day must be inauspicious, and that monkey has come back as a ghost.” Pilgrim came up, grabbed Bajie by the face, and slapped him so hard that he staggered. “You oaf! What ghost am I supposed to be?” The idiot covered his face and said, “Brother, that fiend truly ate you. H-how did you come back to life?” Pilgrim said, “Do you take me for a useless good-for-nothing like you? Once he ate me, I clawed at his bowels and squeezed his lungs, then threaded this rope around his heart and pulled until the pain was unbearable. They all kowtowed and begged for mercy before I spared his life. Now they are bringing a sedan chair to escort my master across the mountain.” When Tripitaka heard this, he scrambled to his feet and bowed to Pilgrim. “Disciple, you have exhausted yourself on my behalf. Had I believed Wuneng’s words, all hope would have been lost.” Pilgrim raised his fist to strike Bajie and cursed, “This bran-guzzling idiot is utterly lazy and thoroughly worthless. Master, do not be upset. The fiends will soon come to escort you.” Sha Monk too felt deeply ashamed. He hurriedly covered up what they had been doing, repacked the luggage, and saddled the horse. Then they all waited on the road, of which there is no more to tell.

p.src: Now the three demon chiefs led their host of fiends back to the cave. The second fiend said, “Elder Brother, I had imagined that Sun Pilgrim was some creature with nine heads and eight tails, but he turned out to be no more than a tiny monkey. You should never have swallowed him. Had we simply fought him, how could he possibly have prevailed against us? There are tens of thousands of fiends in this cave; we could drown him merely by spitting on him. But you swallowed him into your belly, allowing him to work his magic and torment you. How could you contend with him then? Our promise just now to escort the Tang Monk was entirely false. We deceived him into coming out only because your life mattered most. We certainly shall not escort the monk.” The old fiend asked, “Worthy brother, why should we not escort him?” The second fiend said, “Give me three thousand lesser fiends to form a battle array, and I have a way to capture that monkey.” The old fiend said, “Never mind three thousand—you may take the whole camp if you wish. So long as you capture him, we shall all share the merit.”

p.src: The second demon immediately mustered three thousand lesser fiends and went straight to the roadside to form ranks. He ordered a blue-banner bearer to go back and forth proclaiming, “Sun Pilgrim, come out at once and fight our Second Great King!” Hearing this, Bajie laughed. “Brother, as the saying goes, ‘You cannot hide a lie from the locals.’ You have come back playing tricks and deceiving us. How could you say you had subdued the fiends and that they would bring a sedan chair to escort Master, when now they have come to challenge us again?” Pilgrim said, “The old fiend has already been subdued by me and dares not show his face. Even hearing the word ‘Sun’ makes his head ache. This must be the second demon, who resents having to escort us and has therefore issued the challenge. Listen, brothers: these fiends are three brothers, and they show such loyalty to one another; the three of us are brothers too—have we no loyalty at all? I have already subdued the eldest demon. Now that the second has come out, there is no reason you should not fight him.” Bajie said, “Why should I fear him? Just wait while I go fight him.” Pilgrim said, “If you want to go, then go.” Bajie laughed. “Brother, I shall go, but lend me that rope of yours to use.” Pilgrim asked, “What do you want it for? You have neither the ability to crawl into his belly nor the skill to fasten it around his heart. What use could it be to you?” Bajie said, “I want to tie it around my waist as a lifeline. You and Sha Monk hold the other end and let me go out to fight him. If it looks as though I am winning, loosen the rope and I shall capture him; but if I lose to him, pull me back and do not let him drag me away.” Pilgrim secretly laughed to himself. “I may as well play a trick on this idiot.” So he fastened the rope around Bajie’s waist and egged him on to battle.

p.src: The fool raised his rake and ran up the mountainside, shouting, “Come out, demons, and fight your ancestor Zhu!” The blue-banner bearer hastily reported, “Great King, a long-snouted, big-eared monk has come.” The second demon immediately came out of camp. The moment he saw Bajie, without a word, he leveled his spear and thrust it straight at his face; the fool raised his rake and advanced to meet him. The two joined battle before the slope, but in fewer than seven or eight rounds the fool’s arms weakened. Unable to withstand the demon, he hurriedly turned his head and cried, “Elder Brother, this is bad! Pull the lifeline! Pull the lifeline!” On this side, when the Great Sage heard him, he instead slackened the rope and tossed it away. The fool, defeated, turned and fled. While the rope had been dragging taut behind him, he had not noticed it; but when he turned back, its slackness made it tangle around his feet. He tripped and fell, scrambled up, and fell again. At first he merely staggered, but afterward he fell flat on his face. The demon overtook him, unfurled his trunk, and, like a flood dragon, wrapped it around Bajie and carried him triumphantly back to the cave. All the demons sang songs of victory and surged home together.

At first he merely staggered, but afterward he fell flat on his face.
The demon overtook him, unfurled his trunk, and, like a flood dragon, wrapped it around Bajie and carried him triumphantly back to the cave.
All the demons sang songs of victory and surged home together.

p.src: Seeing this from below the slope, Tripitaka again rebuked the Pilgrim: “Wukong, no wonder Wuneng curses you to die! So there is not the least brotherly affection in you—your heart is filled only with jealousy and spite. He told you so plainly to pull the lifeline. Why did you not pull it, but throw the rope away instead? Now that you have let him come to harm, what are we to do?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Master, you are far too indulgent and partial. When old Monkey was captured, you showed not the slightest concern, as though I were nothing but a life to be thrown away; yet the moment this fool is caught, you blame me. Let him suffer a little; then he will understand how difficult it is to fetch the scriptures.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, when you go, how could I not worry? I know you possess transformations and surely will not come to bodily harm. But that fool is clumsy and cannot soar through the air. Now that he has gone, misfortune is far likelier than good fortune. Go and rescue him, I beg you.” The Pilgrim said, “Master, do not complain about me. Wait here while I go and rescue him.”

p.src: He sprang up at once and hurried after them into the mountain, thinking resentfully, “That fool cursed me to die, so I will not make things easy for him yet. I will follow along and see what the demon does to him. After he has suffered a little, I will rescue him.” He formed a hand seal and recited a spell, shook himself, and changed into a tiny insect. Flying off, he settled at the root of Bajie’s ear and entered the cave with the demons. The second demon led three thousand lesser fiends, with drums and music blaring, to the cave entrance, where they encamped. He personally carried Bajie inside and said, “Elder Brother, I have captured one of them.” The old demon said, “Bring him here and let me see.” The other relaxed his trunk, threw Bajie down, and said, “Is this not one of them?” The old demon said, “This fellow is useless.” Hearing this, Bajie said, “Great King, if I am useless, let me go and capture someone useful instead.” The third demon said, “Useless though he may be, he is still Zhu Bajie, a disciple of the Tang Monk. Tie him up for now and put him to soak in the pond at the back. When his bristles have soaked off, cut open his belly, salt and dry him, and save him as a relish for wine on rainy days.” Bajie cried in alarm, “It is all over! I have run into a demon who deals in salted meat!” The fiends all set upon the fool, bound his four limbs together like a horse’s hooves, and, heaving and carrying him, took him to the pond. They pushed him into the middle and all turned away.

p.src: The Great Sage flew up to look. The fool lay with all four limbs pointing skyward and his snout thrust out, half floating and half submerged, puffing and snorting through his mouth. He truly looked ridiculous—just like a great black lotus seedpod in the eighth or ninth month, after frost had made it shed its seeds. Seeing his sorry appearance, the Great Sage both hated and pitied him, and said to himself, “What am I to do with him? He too is one destined to attend the Dragon Flower Assembly. But I cannot forgive him for always wanting to divide the luggage and break up the company, and for urging Master to recite the Tight-Fillet Spell against me. The other day I heard Friar Sand say that he had put aside some private savings. I wonder whether he truly has any. Let me frighten him and find out.”

p.src: Our fine Great Sage flew close to his ear, disguised his voice, and called, “Zhu Wuneng! Zhu Wuneng!” Bajie panicked. “What rotten luck! Guanyin Bodhisattva gave me the name Wuneng, and since I began following the Tang Monk I have also been called Bajie. How can anyone here know that my name is Wuneng?” Unable to contain himself, the fool asked, “Who is calling my religious name?” The Pilgrim said, “It is I.” The fool asked, “Who are you?” The Pilgrim said, “I am an officer sent to summon the dead.” The fool panicked and said, “Officer, where have you come from?” The Pilgrim replied, “The Fifth King of Hell sent me to fetch you.” The fool said, “Officer, please go back and report to the Fifth King of Hell that he is very good friends with my elder brother Sun Wukong. Ask him to spare me for one day and come to fetch me tomorrow.” The Pilgrim said, “Nonsense! ‘If King Yama decrees that one shall die at the third watch, who dares keep him alive until the fourth?’ Come with me at once, and spare yourself being noosed and dragged away.” The fool said, “Officer, can you not do me this favor? Look at the state I am in, and still I want to live. Die I certainly must, but wait just one day until these demons capture my master and companions too. Once I have seen them, all our accounts can be settled together.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly and said, “Very well. There are thirty people on my warrant, scattered hereabouts before and behind us. If I first arrest them and then come for you, there will be a day’s delay. Do you have any traveling money? Give me a little of it.” Bajie said, “Have pity! How could a monk possess any traveling money?” The Pilgrim said, “If you have no traveling money, I shall put the noose on you and take you with me.” The fool panicked. “Officer, do not put the noose on me. I know that rope of yours is called the Life-Chasing Rope; once it is around me, I shall stop breathing. I have some, I have some! I do have a little, though not much.” The Pilgrim said, “Where is it? Bring it out quickly.” Bajie said, “Have pity, have pity! Since I became a monk, some devout households have offered meals to the clergy. Seeing how much I eat, they gave me a little more alms money than the others, and I saved it here bit by bit, until I had five mace of silver. As the bits were hard to keep, the last time we entered a city I asked a silversmith to melt them into one piece. But the heartless fellow stole several candareens from me, leaving me only one lump weighing four mace and six candareens. You may take it.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “This fool does not even have trousers to wear. Where can he have hidden it? Hey! Where is your silver?” Bajie said, “It is stuffed into my left ear. I am tied up and cannot take it out, so help yourself.”

p.src: At these words, Pilgrim reached into the hollow of his ear and drew it out. It really was a small saddle-shaped piece of silver, weighing fully four and a half mace or more. Holding it in his hand, he could not help bursting into loud laughter. Recognizing Pilgrim's voice, the Idiot cursed wildly from the water: “Damn you, stable-tending ape! Even in misery like this, you still come swindling me out of my property!” Pilgrim laughed again. “You filthy glutton! Old Sun has suffered untold hardships protecting Master, while you have been hoarding private savings!” “Shameless wretch!” said Bajie. “What private savings are these? I scraped together every bit of it from between my teeth, denying myself food so I could save enough to buy cloth for a robe—and now you have frightened it out of me. Give me at least some of it back.” “You will not get even half a candareen,” said Pilgrim. Bajie cursed, “Keep it as the price of my life, then! But you had better get me out of here!” “Do not fret,” said Pilgrim. “I will rescue you.” He hid the silver away, resumed his true form, drew his iron staff, and pulled the Idiot close with it. Seizing him by the feet, he hauled him up and untied his ropes. Bajie sprang up, stripped off his clothes, wrung out the water, shook them, and put them back on still damp. “Brother,” he said, “let us leave by the back gate.” “What progress would we have made if we left by the back gate?” said Pilgrim. “We are going out through the front gate.” “My legs are numb from the ropes,” said Bajie. “I cannot run.” “Hurry and follow me,” said Pilgrim.

p.src: The Great Sage was magnificent: wielding his iron staff and displaying its techniques all the way, he fought his way out. The Idiot endured the numbness and had no choice but to stay close behind him. At the second gate he saw his rake leaning against the wall. He went forward, shoved the little fiends aside, snatched it up, and struck wildly ahead. Together with Pilgrim he fought through three or four gates, killing no one knew how many little fiends. Hearing the commotion, the elder demon said to the second, “A fine captive you caught! A fine captive indeed! Look! Sun Pilgrim has rescued Zhu Bajie and is wounding our little fiends at the gates!” The second demon leapt up at once, snatched his spear into his hand, and raced out through the gate. “Insolent ape!” he shouted. “How dare you behave so rudely and hold us in contempt?” The Great Sage heard him, answered the challenge, and stopped. The monster gave him no chance to speak, but thrust at him with the spear. Pilgrim, a true master who never lost his composure, drew his iron staff and met him head-on. Outside the cave gate, the two fought a splendid battle:

p.src: When Bajie saw the Great Sage fighting the demon, he stood on the mountain spur with his rake upright. He did not come to help, but merely stared stupidly at them. The demon found Pilgrim's staff heavy and his technique flawless, with no opening anywhere. Holding off the staff with his spear, he unfurled his trunk and tried to coil it around him. Pilgrim knew what he was about. Gripping the gold-banded staff in both hands, he held it crosswise and raised it overhead. The demon's trunk coiled around his waist and hips, but failed to bind his hands. Just look at him, twirling his staff playfully with both hands above the demon's trunk! Seeing this, Bajie beat his chest and cried, “Well now! What rotten luck that monster has! When he coiled around a clumsy fool like me, he caught my hands too, so I could not move at all. Yet when he coils around one as slippery as that, he leaves his hands free. With that staff in his hands, he need only jab it into the trunk. Once the nostril hurts and starts streaming, how could the monster possibly keep him bound?”

p.src: Pilgrim had not originally thought of this; it was Bajie who gave him the idea. He shook the staff, making it as slender as an egg yet over ten feet long, and truly jabbed it into the demon's nostril. The demon took fright and, with a hiss, abruptly released his trunk. Pilgrim twisted around, seized the trunk in one hand, and pulled forward with all his strength. Afraid of worsening the pain, the demon yielded to his grip and stepped along behind him. Only then did Bajie dare approach. Raising his rake, he struck wildly at the demon's haunches. “No, no!” said Pilgrim. “The teeth of that rake are sharp. If you break his skin and draw blood, Master will see it and accuse us again of harming life. Turn it around and beat him with the handle instead.”

p.src: The Idiot really did raise the rake handle, taking one step and dealing one blow. Pilgrim led the demon by the trunk, and the two of them looked just like elephant handlers as they brought him down the slope. Tripitaka was gazing anxiously into the distance. When he saw the two approaching amid a great commotion, he called, “Wujing, look! What is Wukong leading?” Sha Monk looked and laughed. “Master, Eldest Brother is dragging the demon here by the nose. What a delightful sight!” “Mercy!” said Tripitaka. “Mercy! What a huge demon, and what a long trunk he has! Ask him this: if he will gladly escort us across the mountain, you may pardon him. Do not take his life.” Sha Monk hurried forward to meet them and shouted, “Master says that if the monster will truly escort him across the mountain, you are not to harm his life!” Hearing this, the monster hastily knelt and mumbled his assent. Pilgrim had been gripping his trunk so tightly that his voice was stopped up, making him sound like someone with a terrible cold. He called, “Reverend Tang, if you will spare my life, I shall have a sedan chair brought at once and escort you onward.” “We master and disciples are all compassionate and merciful people,” said Pilgrim. “We will take you at your word and spare your life for now. Bring the sedan chair quickly. If you change your mind again and we catch you, we shall show no further mercy.” Released from his grasp, the monster kowtowed and departed. Pilgrim and Bajie went to see the Tang Monk and gave him a full account of all that had happened. Overwhelmed with shame, Bajie spread his clothes to dry before the slope and waited there. We shall speak no more of them for now.

p.src: Trembling with fear, the second demon returned to the cave. Before he arrived, little fiends had already informed the elder and third demons that Pilgrim had dragged the second demon away by the trunk. Alarmed, the elder demon and the third had just led their forces out when they saw the second returning alone. They all welcomed him inside and asked why he had been released. The second demon repeated to them all Tripitaka's compassionate and merciful words. They stared at one another, and not one of them dared speak. The second demon asked, “Elder Brother, shall we escort the Tang Monk?” “Brother, what are you saying?” replied the elder demon. “Sun Pilgrim is a generous and righteous ape. When he was inside my belly, he could have killed a thousand of me if he had wished to take my life. And just now, when he seized your trunk, if he had dragged you away without releasing you, a mere squeeze would have crushed its tip. That is a frightening thought indeed. Hurry and make preparations to escort him onward.” The third demon laughed. “Escort him, escort him, escort him!” “Worthy Brother,” said the elder demon, “those words sound rather like a fit of pique. If you will not escort him, the two of us shall do it.”

p.src: The third demon laughed again and said, “Elder brothers, if that monk declines our escort and we simply deceive him this way, then it will be his good fortune; but if he asks us to escort him, he will have fallen squarely into my stratagem of luring the tiger away from the mountain.” The eldest demon asked, “What do you mean by ‘luring the tiger away from the mountain’?” The third demon replied, “We shall muster all the fiends in the cave, choose a thousand from ten thousand, a hundred from the thousand, then select sixteen—and another thirty—from the hundred.” The eldest demon asked, “Why do you need both sixteen and thirty?” The third demon said, “The thirty must know how to cook. Give them fine rice and flour, bamboo shoots, tender tea leaves, fragrant mushrooms, other mushrooms, bean curd, and wheat gluten. Have them set up shelters every twenty or thirty li, prepare tea and meals, and entertain the Tang Monk.” The eldest demon asked, “And what use are the sixteen?” The third demon replied, “Eight will carry the sedan chair, and eight will clear the road with cries. We three brothers will accompany them on either side and escort him for part of the journey. A little over four hundred li west of here lies my city, where troops stand ready to support us. When we reach the city’s edge, we shall do thus and so, leaving master and disciples unable to look after both front and rear. The success of our attempt to capture the Tang Monk will depend entirely upon those sixteen.” The eldest demon was overjoyed when he heard this; it was truly as though he had just awakened from drunkenness or roused from a dream. “Excellent! Excellent! Excellent!” he cried. He at once mustered the fiends, first choosing thirty and giving them the provisions; then he chose sixteen more to carry a fragrant rattan sedan chair, and they all went out together. He also instructed the other fiends, “None of you may wander idly upon the mountain. Sun the Pilgrim is a suspicious monkey; if he sees you coming and going, he will certainly grow wary and see through our plan.”

The success of our attempt to capture the Tang Monk will depend entirely upon those sixteen.”
The eldest demon was overjoyed when he heard this;
it was truly as though he had just awakened from drunkenness or roused from a dream.
“Excellent! Excellent! Excellent!” he cried.
He at once mustered the fiends, first choosing thirty and giving them the provisions;
then he chose sixteen more to carry a fragrant rattan sedan chair, and they all went out together.

He also instructed the other fiends, “None of you may wander idly upon the mountain. Sun the Pilgrim is a suspicious monkey; if he sees you coming and going, he will certainly grow wary and see through our plan.”

p.src: The eldest demon then led the company to the roadside and called loudly, “Venerable Master Tang, there will be no red sand today. Please cross the mountain without delay.” Tripitaka heard him and asked, “Wukong, who is calling me?” The Pilgrim pointed and said, “Over there are the fiends I subdued. They have brought a sedan chair to escort you.” Tripitaka pressed his palms together and raised them toward Heaven, saying, “Blessed indeed! Blessed indeed! Without the great abilities of such a worthy disciple, how could I ever have passed this way?” He went straight forward, saluted the fiends, and said, “I am deeply grateful for your kindness. When my disciples and I return eastward from fetching the scriptures to Chang’an, we shall proclaim the merit of your good deed.” The fiends kowtowed and said, “Please enter the sedan chair, Venerable Master.” Tripitaka, being but mortal flesh with ordinary eyes, did not know it was a trick. The Great Sage Sun, though an immortal of the Grand Monad, was upright and loyal by nature. He merely believed that by alternately capturing and releasing them he had subdued the fiends; how could he have expected them all to harbor treachery? Thus he made no close investigation and yielded entirely to his master’s wishes. He ordered Bajie to secure the luggage upon the horse and follow closely with Sha Monk. He himself wielded his iron staff and went ahead to clear the road, watching on every side for good or ill. Eight fiends raised the sedan chair, eight cried out in turn to clear the road, and the three demon kings walked beside the carrying poles. The master sat upright in the sedan chair, delighted and content. They climbed the high mountain and proceeded along the main road.

p.src: Little did they know that on this journey sorrow would arise once more amid their joy. As the classic says, “When prosperity reaches its height, adversity is born anew.” When fate brings one face-to-face with the baleful Grand Duke, the stars of Mourning Gate and Funeral Guest appear as well. That band of fiends guarded them on either side with one heart and purpose, attending them diligently morning and evening. After thirty li they offered a vegetarian meal, and after another fifty li yet another; before evening they invited the pilgrims to rest, and everything along the road was perfectly orderly. Three meals a day satisfied their every wish; and each pleasant night they lodged in comfortable quarters.

p.src: While the Great Sage was still gripped by alarm, he suddenly heard the wind whistle behind his ears. He turned his head in haste and saw the third demon raising a painted-shaft square-bladed halberd in both hands and striking at his head. The Great Sage quickly rolled over, sprang to his feet, and met the blow head-on with his gold-banded cudgel. Both were seething with anger, and neither wasted another word; gritting their teeth, each was determined to prevail. Then the eldest demon gave the signal, raised his steel saber, and hacked at Bajie. Bajie panicked, abandoned the horse, swung his rake, and struck wildly ahead. The second demon leveled his long spear and thrust it at Sha Monk. Sha Monk wielded his demon-quelling staff, took his stance, and held him off. Thus the three demon chiefs and the three monks, each matched against one opponent, fought desperately upon the mountain, heedless of life and death.

p.src: The sixteen lesser fiends, meanwhile, obeyed their orders and each performed his part. They seized the white horse and the luggage, crowded around Tripitaka, and carried the sedan chair straight to the city gate, crying loudly, “The grand kings’ plan has succeeded! We have captured the Tang Monk!” Every fiend in the city, great and small, ran down and flung the city gates wide open. Orders went out to every camp to furl the banners and silence the drums, and no one was permitted to shout or beat the gongs. They said, “The grand kings gave orders beforehand that the Tang Monk must not be frightened. The Tang Monk cannot endure a fright. One scare will sour his flesh and make it unfit to eat.” All the fiends joyfully welcomed Tripitaka, bowing low and bending their backs as they received the venerable monk. They carried the Tang Monk, sedan chair and all, into the golden throne hall, invited him to sit in the center, and bustled around him on every side, offering tea and food. The elder was dazed and bewildered, and wherever he looked he saw not a single friendly face.
